body.heading: Your hand is a calendar
paragraphs: Make a fist and look at your knuckles. Starting at the first knuckle (your index finger's), count the months across the bumps and dips: knuckle, dip, knuckle, dip. Every month that lands on a knuckle has 31 days. Every month in a dip has 30 — with one famous exception.

January is a knuckle: 31 days. February is a dip — and it is the exception, with 28 days (29 in a leap year). March is a knuckle again: 31. Continue across one hand to July, then start again on the first knuckle for August — which is why July and August, two knuckles in a row if you use both fists side by side, both have 31 days.

body.heading: The rhyme that backs it up
paragraphs: If knuckles are not handy, the old rhyme does the same job: 'Thirty days hath September, April, June and November; all the rest have thirty-one…' — except February, which the rhyme treats as the special case it is.
Between the knuckles and the rhyme you have two independent memory systems — one in your body, one in your ears. Facts stored in two places are facts you actually keep.

body.heading: February, the rule-breaker
paragraphs: February's shortness is a souvenir of the Roman calendar, and its leap day follows a rule worth knowing precisely: a year is a leap year if it divides by 4 — except century years, which are leap years only if they divide by 400. So 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 was not.
Teach the knuckle trick to someone younger this week. It takes thirty seconds, it works forever, and it needs no battery — the best kind of technology there is.

takeaway: Knuckles are 31-day months and the dips are the short ones — your hand has carried a calendar all along.
